title: Experts: How are climate scientists using artificial intelligence? - Carbon Brief
gist: Ten climate and AI researchers describe how AI is used in weather forecasting, satellite monitoring, grid management and policy modelling, with ECMWF already running an AI forecast system alongside its traditional one. They flag key limits: AI underperforms physics models on unprecedented extremes, climate lacks future data, and the benefits and compute are concentrated in the global north.

insights.claim: AI weather-prediction models learn from large volumes of data and feed predictions back into themselves to forecast up to two weeks ahead, delivering accurate predictions with far less computing power than numerical models.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Lower compute cost for forecasting shifts economics toward AI incumbents and weather-data users.
insights.locator: One of the most significant recent developments

insights.claim: The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts is deploying an AI forecast system in its official forecasts alongside the traditional system, and AI systems are now competitive with the world's leading numerical weather prediction.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: AI weather models have moved into operational use at a major forecasting body, a proof point of commercial and institutional adoption.
insights.locator: We’re seeing a really exciting renaissance

insights.claim: AI forecast models do well on typical weather but underperform physics-based models on record-breaking and unprecedented extremes, which are the events that matter most for adaptation.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Insurers and risk modellers should not rely on pure-AI forecasts for tail events.
insights.quote: AI forecast models do well on typical weather, but underperform physics-based models on record-breaking and unprecedented extremes
insights.locator: AI forecast models do well on typical weather

insights.claim: Climate prediction differs from weather forecasting because projections must cover future climates outside the observational record, so the central challenge is where the training data comes from.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: AI success in weather does not transfer directly to long-run climate projection, tempering expectations.
insights.locator: Climate prediction is fundamentally different.

insights.claim: Using AI to emulate or accelerate existing physics-based climate models, rather than purely data-driven approaches, could make climate risk information far more accessible and affordable while retaining confidence in projections.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Cheaper climate risk data creates opportunity for climate analytics providers and financial risk users.
insights.locator: One promising route forward is, therefore

insights.claim: New machine-learning architectures such as diffusion models, foundation models and generative ensembles now reach weather and climate work within months instead of two to three years, and the cost of running a global forecast has dropped by orders of magnitude.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Falling forecast cost widens who can produce weather and climate information, lowering barriers for new entrants.
insights.locator: A few years ago, it took two or three years

insights.claim: AI algorithms scan hyperspectral satellite imagery to pinpoint industrial methane leaks globally and alert operators in near real time.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Automated methane detection feeds oil and gas regulatory and leak-monitoring markets.
insights.locator: Methane tracking and ecosystem monitoring

insights.claim: Machine-learning models process thousands of satellite images daily to detect illegal logging, land-use changes and glacier retreat far faster than humans could review manually.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Supports demand for geospatial-AI monitoring in deforestation and land-use compliance.
insights.locator: At the same time, machine-learning models process

insights.claim: In sea ice research the most mature ML application is extracting more information from observations, while Ice Net was an early demonstration of a deep-learning system outperforming a leading physical model in seasonal Arctic forecasts.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Shows AI beating physics models in a specific domain, though in seasonal Arctic forecasting only.
insights.locator: In sea ice research, machine learning is now used

insights.claim: Machine learning can extract information from ship logs, whaling records, expedition photographs and early aerial imagery to lengthen the Antarctic sea ice record beyond the satellite era that began in 1979.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Longer observational records improve training and testing of AI systems.
insights.locator: Much of what we know about Antarctic sea ice

themes.theme: AI in grids and climate policy

insights.claim: AI is used on power grids to better predict solar and wind production and to optimise and control generators, batteries and flexible loads such as industrial loads and EV batteries.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Forecasting and flexibility software are enabling layers for high-renewable grids.
insights.locator: As we introduce more solar, wind and other renewable energy

insights.claim: AI is useful at three stages of the climate policy cycle: measurement (satellite emissions estimates, air quality), modelling futures (cheap emulators allow thousands of scenarios rather than a handful), and evaluation (causal ML to test whether a policy worked).
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Cheaper scenario modelling enables broader policy and risk analysis for policy-exposed investors.
insights.locator: AI is already useful at every stage of the climate policy cycle.

insights.claim: Reinforcement learning is being used to study how multiple actors such as countries or electricity producers compete and cooperate under different policy designs, revealing strategies classical analysis misses.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: An emerging method for market and policy design simulation.
insights.locator: Reinforcement learning [a type of AI

themes.theme: AI in IPCC and CMIP institutions

insights.claim: The IPCC's seventh assessment includes, for the first time, a model intercomparison project just for AI-based weather and climate models, which William Collins calls a milestone and harbinger of more to come.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Formal inclusion of AI models in the assessment process legitimises them for policy use.
insights.locator: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) is performing

insights.claim: William Collins thinks the IPCC's eighth assessment, likely due in the late 2020s, may largely be written using large language models, with AI's value being to flag what is uncertain or unknown so science knows where to head.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Signals LLM adoption even in scientific synthesis; the IPCC set up an AI informal group in September 2026.
insights.locator: I think the IPCC’s eighth assessment

insights.claim: The eighth Coupled Model Intercomparison Project will have machine-learning codes running alongside traditional climate models, and the WCRP has set up a task team on AI covering modelling, data, private-sector engagement and trustworthiness.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: AI is becoming embedded in the core institutional climate modelling pipeline.
insights.locator: AI will also be an integral part of the eighth

insights.claim: Hybrid modelling that merges physics-based Earth system models with machine-learning speed is expected to overcome computational bottlenecks, replace unresolved subgrid processes and help narrow uncertainties on the terrestrial carbon sink and tipping points.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Hybrid approaches may tighten carbon-sink uncertainty relevant to carbon budgets.
insights.locator: The inclusion of AI in climate and land-vegetation modelling

insights.claim: The large energy and water demands of AI refer to large-scale generative and agentic systems, not mostly to the kinds of AI actually used to fight climate change.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Separates data-centre generative AI energy concerns from narrow climate-science AI use.
insights.locator: People talk a lot about energy usage of AI

insights.claim: The public equates AI with LLMs and chatbots, so people deciding research funding may hold a mismatched understanding and the right science may not get funded.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Funding misallocation risk follows from narrow perceptions of AI.
insights.locator: I think the general public thinks of AI

insights.claim: Frontier models are built almost exclusively in the global north, trained on data densest where observations are richest and validated on benchmarks reflecting the same regions, so cheap inference alone does not fix the gap.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: AI could widen the global divide in climate information access, a policy and equity risk.
insights.locator: Frontier models [which are at the cutting edge

insights.claim: Adapting pre-trained AI-based Earth system models on modest hardware could let small groups or agencies in data-poor regions avoid building bespoke systems, where vulnerability is highest and data thinnest.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Pre-trained models could democratise access if shared deliberately.
insights.locator: If done well, [developing AI-based Earth system models]

insights.claim: The consolidation of large-scale AI can work against equitable climate action by concentrating power in certain geographies and stakeholders and defining action around their goals.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: AI market concentration carries governance implications for climate adaptation.
insights.locator: Climate action should fundamentally be about democratisation

insights.claim: The biggest AI risk in climate science is trust: good performance is not enough without independent evaluation, physical credibility, process-based validation, robustness and some interpretability.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Validation standards will gate adoption of AI models in high-stakes uses.
insights.locator: The biggest challenge is trust

insights.claim: AI's apparent success could be read as a reason to invest less in observations, but AI is no substitute for observation, and Antarctic sea ice needs more targeted observations, not fewer.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Risk of defunding observation networks that AI itself depends on.
insights.locator: The risk I worry about most

insights.claim: AI always gives an answer, so the risk is a plausible but 'truthy' answer that is not the truth, and getting the right answer for the right reason must be verified.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Model output validity checks are essential before using AI projections in decisions.
insights.quote: the risk is getting a plausible answer that is “truthy”, but not the truth
insights.locator: The challenge is always making sure

insights.claim: AI risks diverting attention from other forms of climate action, as it is not a silver bullet and where useful is only one part of the solution.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Be sceptical of AI-as-climate-solution narratives that displace mitigation.
insights.quote: AI is not a silver bullet.
insights.locator: The first and foremost risk

insights.claim: AI tools are leading to many more research proposals being submitted, forcing scientific disciplines to set rules on AI use in writing articles, reviewing and proposals.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: AI-driven volume increase strains peer review and funding processes.
insights.locator: There are now many more proposals being submitted

insights.claim: Partnerships between academia, data centres and private industry will be integral, but must respect open science and open-source code, avoiding closed LLM-style models and ensuring fairness, accountability, transparency and explainability.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Private-compute dependence raises openness and governance questions for climate AI.
insights.locator: The partnership between academia, the data centres

insights.claim: High-resolution AI outputs can look exact when they are not, and uncertainties compound invisibly, so policy-relevant predictions need honest, well-calibrated uncertainty estimates and AI should augment human judgement rather than replace it.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Overprecision in AI downscaled output is a model-risk flag for users of climate data.
insights.locator: High-resolution outputs can look exact
